title: Build an API that answers from sources
audience: Web engineer · a first source-backed service
summary: An API lets other software request work. Build one that finds approved source passages, returns supported answers and reports when evidence is missing.

steps.task: The engineer writes the request and response contract: the fields other software sends and receives. Fictional example: For “reset HH2”, accept productId=HH2 and return the answer plus source identifiers; absent productId returns needs_product.

The source owner identifies approved documents and who may read them. A tenant is a customer organisation with separate private records. Fictional example: Use approved HH2-r3; exclude withdrawn HH2-r2 and tickets outside the signed-in tenant.
The engineer retrieves, or searches for, evidence before asking a model to answer. Fictional example: For “reset HH2”, expect HH2-r3:s4, meaning section s4 of revision r3, in the returned passages.

The subject expert and test engineer prepare a golden dataset: questions with independently reviewed expected results. Fictional example: Q1 needs HH2-r3:s4; Q2 asks “refund policy”, which the reset manual cannot answer. Record that distinction before testing.

The answer reviewer checks each claim against its source. Abstention means explicitly declining to answer without enough evidence. Fictional example: HH2-r3 says 10 seconds, so answer 10 and cite s4; without evidence, say “I cannot establish that from this manual”.

The test engineer records a baseline, the simple starting approach used for comparison. Fictional example: On the same 10 questions, keyword search finds a relevant source for 7: record 7/10 before trying hybrid search, which combines word matching with similarity search.

The service owner assigns a responder and a stop condition before release. Fictional example: One confirmed disclosure between customer organisations disables private-source search and routes users to support. Record who investigates and who may restore access.

title: Give an agent tools with explicit limits
audience: Engineer and product owner · actions and approval
summary: An agent uses a model to choose actions; a tool is an operation it can request. Define approval and failure handling before it can change real records.

steps.task: The product owner defines the task and the real change that counts as success. Fictional example: Prepare replacement HH2 at address A; success is approved order O17, not a convincing message saying it was ordered.

The engineer separates the agent’s repeated decide-and-act loop from the integration code that calls external services. Fictional example: The agent proposes createOrder; the integration checks the account, approved draft revision and idempotency key, a request identifier that prevents duplicate effects.

The engineer writes the allowed workflow states and transitions. Fictional example: Draft r3 → approved r3 → submitted K17 → created O17. If the reply is lost after submission, look up the request status before attempting another action.

The test engineer checks the stored result and sequence of actions. Fictional example: Retry request K17 after a timeout: expect existing order O17 and exactly one stored order, with no second create action.
The product owner and test engineer agree a rubric, the written scoring rules. Fictional example: A pass requires the approved item and address and one order; a friendly reply without an order fails.

The service operator needs records that explain which decision led to each action. Fictional example: Record request K17, draft r3 and order O17. If approval is missing, show that the request stopped before submission.

title: Decide whether a change is better
audience: Decision owner and engineer · evidence for a change
summary: Use reviewed cases to compare versions, understand uncertainty and decide whether the evidence supports release. Completing a test does not itself authorise release.

steps.task: The decision owner and subject expert define the cost of each wrong result. Fictional example: The wrong HH2 reset duration can cause failure; disclosing another customer organisation’s ticket is a separate defect that blocks release.

The subject expert supplies cases with expected outcomes for a golden dataset, a versioned reference for checks. Fictional example: Q1 asks reset HH2 (10 seconds); Q2 lacks the product (ask for it); Q3 requests another organisation’s ticket (deny access).

The test engineer separates development cases from held-out cases, which remain unseen until final evaluation. Fictional example: Put ticket T1 and all its messages in development; keep T2 and its replies together in the unseen group.

The subject expert and reviewers agree a rubric, the written rules for deciding a pass. Fictional example: “Hold Reset 10 seconds” is supported by HH2-r3:s4; “5 seconds” fails even when it cites the same section.

The test engineer calibrates an automated judge by comparing its labels with independent human labels. Fictional example: Among 10 answers, 2 marked supported by the judge are unsupported according to people. Inspect those false positives, or incorrect positive labels, before trusting its scores.

The analyst compares both versions on the same cases and calculates uncertainty in the difference. Fictional example: A passes 80/100 and B 84/100. With 10 B-only passes and 6 A-only passes, B gains +4 percentage points; the estimate still needs an uncertainty calculation.

The release owner records pass conditions, remaining decisions and the responder’s stop authority. Fictional example: Require no observed disclosure between customer organisations; any confirmed disclosure after release disables private-source search. This sample result does not prove failure is impossible.

title: Change a model and plan how to run it
summary: Compare changes to prompts, learned model parameters and hosting. Keep final evaluation cases unseen while developing the change.

steps.task: The engineer records the baseline, the current approach, with quality, cost and delay. Fictional example: 80/100 correct, EUR 4 per 100 requests and p95 latency 2 seconds, the delay at the 95th percentile of requests.

The product owner names the error the change should reduce. Optimisation means changing instructions or model parameters to improve a measured result. Fictional example: Reduce unsupported answers on the same 100-case comparison; reject a change that adds disclosure between customer organisations.

The test engineer keeps training, development and final test groups separate. Fictional example: Train on tickets T1–T20, develop on T21–T25 and hold out T26–T30 for final evaluation. Keep every ticket’s replies in its group.

The subject expert reviews synthetic data, which is produced by a generator and can repeat its errors. Fictional example: Generated HH2 answers all say 5 seconds, but independent source HH2-r3 says 10. Reject the generated labels.

The hosting engineer tests simultaneous requests and assigns an incident responder before access is enabled. Fictional example: At concurrency 10, meaning requests in progress together, with 1000-token prompts, the proposed p95 first-token limit is 2 seconds. Tokens are pieces of text; first-token delay ends when output starts.

Finance and the product owner compare quality gains with full service cost. Fictional example: Failures fall 20→16 per 100 requests while cost rises EUR 4→8. Compare EUR 4 extra with the agreed value of four corrected outcomes before deciding.
